segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we've seen how two sounds in the verbs in the present tense might split when we put pressure on them.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We've seen how e might become ie. So, for example, we have querer, which means to want, but I want is?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero. So we stress down on that e, and it splits into ie. And this will happen for the other versions that we learned as well. So how do you say he wants, or she wants, or you formal want?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So another example where this will happen is with the verb perder, which means to lose—it's related to perish. So how would you say I lose?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pierdo, good. And he loses, she loses?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we saw that the e can split into ie, and we also saw that an o in the base of the verb can split into ue.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we saw, for example, poder is to be able, and then we have puedo, I can, I am able. We had dormir. What did dormir mean?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What changed when we added me: me duermo?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I think it's I fall asleep.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. I sleep myself, I fall asleep. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we can expect to see these o's split, but not always. For example, to eat was?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Como. So it didn't split there. So there's no way to know where it will, where it won't. Most of the time it will, and you just have to kind of experiment and see what happens, and you will always get the feedback when you try to see if it splits or not. You will also develop an intuition of where you should do it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So colgar, for example, is to hang. So if you want to say I hang?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuelga. Why do you think you said cuelgue first?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, the reason you explained before with the it sounds like, because it has an e sound before, it seems to go more.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. It fits more. So you will find yourself doing that. How do you get out of doing that? How do you stop that happening?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: By going back to the to version of the verb.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. And then you're in control. Colgar, -ar verb, cuelga. Good. They hang?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Words in English that begin al-, so not end -al like normal, normal, metal, metal; if they begin al-, they come from Arabic. This al- means "the" in Arabic. And in Arabic it's written with the word; it's written as one word, it's all stuck together. So when words came in from Arabic, they kind of came in most of the time with this al-, which meant "the".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, for example, alcohol. And when we say the alcohol, we are actually saying something like the the alcohol, something like this. The verb to take is tomar. Tomar, t-o-m-a-r.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tomar. And this is also used like to drink. So it's used like take generically, generally, but also to drink. How would you say I don't drink alcohol, I don't take alcohol?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, no tomo alcohol. Sugar in Spanish is azúcar. Azúcar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Azúcar. Or in Spain, because we have a z here, it would be azúcar in most of Spain. Now, this is also an Arabic word, and it's the same word as sugar in English, might not look like it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What's happened here? In Arabic, the l of al-, the word for "the", assimilates, changes to match the next letter if the next letter is kind of close to it. It does this with about half the letters. So in Arabic, actually, instead of al-sukkar, you say as-sukkar. And this passed into Spanish. But in English, we got the word without the "the" at the beginning this time. This time sugar came in without the "the" at the beginning, so they look kind of different and sound rather different—sugar, azúcar—but again, they're the same word.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say I don't take sugar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No tomo azúcar. Arroz, rice, is also an Arabic word. It's actually al-ruzz, the rice. But again, in Spanish the l assimilated to the next r, as it does in Arabic. And instead of al-ruzz, like in Arabic ar-ruzz, we ended up with arroz.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So is azúcar, azúcar with two s's?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, it's with a z here, because two s's are not a combination you find in Spanish. So, for example, in the word possible, we have two s's there in English, but in Spanish when we write posible we write one s. The same with passion, we write one s in Spanish: pasión. So you don't get two s's together in Spanish, but you do get two r's together to differentiate between the normal r and the rolling r.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in Spanish we have a-r-r-o-z. It's just assimilation of al-ruzz, ar-ruzz to Spanish arroz, and it's the same word as English rice. So how would you say I want rice?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero arroz, good. Algebra, how would that be in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Álgebra, good. Spanish has a lot more Arabic than English. The south of Spain was part of the Muslim world for 800 years, so the languages had a lot of contact. And you get more words in Spanish that you don't have in English that are from Arabic. So, for example, aceite, oil—in Arabic this is zayt—aceite. Aceituna, olive—zaytun, zaytūn in Arabic. Alfombra, which means carpet; almohada, which means pillow. All of these words they came in from Arabic. When you find al- at the beginning, with maybe a couple of exceptions, it's from Arabic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we said I take is tomo. How is he takes, she takes, it takes, you formal take?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Toma, good. You informal, talking to a friend?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say what are you taking? This could be a way to ask what do you want to drink?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Qué tomas? To drink exists, it's beber. Beber. And the word drink, the noun, una bebida, a drink—una, we have a for feminine words—una bebida or la bebida, the drink, comes from beber. But tomar, to take, is extremely common.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Toman, good. Now, there's one more version of the verbs that we didn't learn yet, which was the we version. We didn't learn how to say we want or we have.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, we take is tomamos. Tomamos. Explain to me what I did then to get we take. If I go from tomar to tomamos, what am I doing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: You took out the -r and put a -mos at the end.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But to make it fit in with your—

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Well, you took out the -ar, the "ar" sound—

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: —sound. This is very nice to think about it this way because then you fit it in with what you've been doing up until now, taking off the -ar, a-r, and putting on your ending. So you take off -ar and you put on -amos, and you get the we form.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablamos, good. So with -amos, we are adding on two syllables, and the accent is going on the second-to-last syllable. So it's in a different position, the accent, to the other versions. If we look at tomo, toma, toman, tomas, tomamos, the accent's moving. Again, to speak?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablamos, good. So this affects the split of the e or the o in the root of the verb, because we said that it splits because you stress it, but in the we form we don't actually stress it. So let's look at this. What was to find or to encounter?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encuentro. I find or I'm finding. He finds?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encuentra, good. You went back to the "to" form, right?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now, we, you're not stressing that o anymore so it's safe. It's not going to split.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good, encontramos. We don't stress it so it doesn't split. What was demonstration?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Demostración. So how would you say to demonstrate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Demostrar. If you take away this de-, which actually means "of" in Spanish, if you get rid of it you're left with mostrar, and what does mostrar mean?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To show. I show or I'm showing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mostro— it should be mostro, but muestro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, muestro. And he or she, it, you formal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good, mostramos. You're not accenting anymore that o, so it doesn't split: mostramos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you say to think? And we said it's related to the word pensive.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pienso. There the e splits when we stress it. If you want to say I think so, you can just say I think that yes. I think that yes. "That" is the same as what?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pienso que sí. I think so: pienso que sí. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He thinks or she thinks, you formal think?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. If you say what do you think to do, we said that this means what do you plan on doing. You can just say what do you think to do. What was to do? To do or to make, which begins with a silent h?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hacer, good. So what do you think to do? What do you plan on doing?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, how would you say we think?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, pensamos. So you're not splitting there: pensamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The verb to close, to close is cerrar. C-e-r-r-a-r, cerrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Or in most of Spain, cerrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say I close?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cierro, good. She closes, he closes, you formal close?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cierra, good. So how would you say we close?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we're seeing that really this issue of the e's and the o's splitting is an issue about stress, and it's only when we stress them down that they split under that pressure. When we don't, they are intact. They stay intact.
